question: The Commission is preparing an action plan for the digitalisation of the water sector1, including the widespread deployment of smart meters for all2 and the use of IoT and AI technologies. While these technologies are designed to help save water and detect leaks, the collection of detailed household consumption data gives rise to the risk of profiling, commercial exploitation and automated decision-making.

Water is a natural resource, a ‘shared resource’ as the European Parliament put it, not a mere commercial product. Access to drinking water for all is provided for under Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2020/2184. At the same time, Article 17 requires compliance with applicable data protection rules3. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it ensure that smart meter data is not used for unnecessary profiling, commercialisation or transmission to third parties?
Will it take measures to ensure that smart meters, algorithms and AI do not lead to the automated restriction or interruption of water supply, in particular as a result of financial hardship?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.11.2026) The Commission attaches great importance to ensuring that the digitalisation of the water sector contributes to sustainability, resilience and improved service delivery.

As regards the use of smart meter data, the Commission considers that the deployment of smart water meters and related digital tools must be accompanied by robust safeguards governing the collection, processing and use of data.

Data protection is a fundamental right in the EU, and the applicable EU data protection framework1, including the General Data Protection Regulation2 where personal data are concerned, must be fully respected.

The increasing use of smart meters, algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI) in the water sector offers significant opportunities but also calls for appropriate safeguards to prevent potential misuse or unintended disruptions to service provision. As critical infrastructure, the water sector needs to remain resilient to a range of evolving risks.

The AI systems used in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, including water supply, should they be classified as high-risk, they become subject to specific safeguarding requirements under the AI Act3, notably as regards risk management, human oversight and accountability. The forthcoming Action Plan on the Digitalisation of the Water Sector4 will reflect these key principles.

The Action Plan is currently under drafting. The call for evidence and consultation activities carried out to date have already identified several central priorities, including digital protection of critical water infrastructure, the trustworthy and secure use of digital technologies, improved data governance and cybersecurity.

1 https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/legal-framework-eu-data-protection_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pp. 1–88.

3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act), OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024. 4 https://environment.ec.
